strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 41 diverse downstream tasks in 56 cities with proper experimental methodology and cross-regional generalization testing
Well-motivated theoretical framework using Partial Information Decomposition (PID) to justify combining contrastive learning with reconstruction loss for multimodal fusion
Practical robustness demonstrated through handling incomplete multimodal data via stochastic masking, with ablation studies showing minimal degradation with limited modalities
Extensive ablation studies (Tables 6-12) systematically validate contributions of individual components and architectural choices
Strong empirical results showing consistent improvements over GeoFM, GeCLIP, and SatCLIP baselines across diverse geospatial prediction tasks
Valuable contribution to the community through PPM-2 dataset release with 110,988 locations and multi-modal data
High reproducibility standards with detailed implementation specifics, dataset documentation, and promise of code release
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—individual components (contrastive learning, reconstruction loss, multimodal fusion) are well-established; contribution is primarily in their combination for this application
Theoretical contribution (Lemma 1) is straightforward and relies on strong assumptions (Assumption 1) whose necessity in practice is not validated
Inconsistent improvements across tasks with some showing only 1-2 percentage point gains; insufficient analysis of when/why the method fails or which task characteristics determine its effectiveness
Statistical significance testing largely absent; confidence intervals inconsistently reported; no significance testing of performance differences
Evaluation exclusively on PP2M dataset; generalization to other urban datasets and geospatial benchmarks not demonstrated
Geographic bias in dataset (concentration in developed nations) and missing ethical discussion of surveillance/privacy implications and potential perpetuation of socioeconomic biases
Insufficient justification of design choices (e.g., z-score normalization for 'equal contribution', specific masking strategy) and lack of ablation comparing alternative approaches
Computational overhead (6.57ms inference vs 4-5ms for baselines) not thoroughly discussed despite non-negligible cost
Dense presentation (58 pages) with key details relegated to appendices; intuition before formalism lacking in technical sections
Synthetic data experiments (Section D.2) somewhat contrived; difficulty in assigning information dimensions to real multimodal data limits insights

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 41 tasks in 56 cities with extensive ablation studies (Sections D.1-D.8) demonstrating systematic investigation
Well-organized framework combining contrastive learning with latent modality reconstruction, with formal theoretical grounding including proofs of information preservation
Strong reproducibility efforts including planned code/data release and detailed implementation documentation in appendix
Addresses practical problem of multimodal spatial representation learning with clear motivation and application relevance
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (contrastive learning, reconstruction loss, random masking) without fundamental methodological innovation; SMF framework is essentially random subset sampling + CL + reconstruction

Weak theoretical justification: Assumption 1 (demanding proxy modality exists for each task) is strong and never empirically validated; no justification for why random masking is superior to alternatives

Unfair experimental setup: different methods trained on different datasets (PP2-M vs MP-16 vs S2-100k), and Identity baseline achieves -66.0 R² on Housing Prices suggesting flawed comparison; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported

Marginal empirical improvements: many results appear within noise margins (e.g., UrbanFusion 78.7% vs GAIR 78.5% for Housing Prices); cross-regional generalization (Table 4) shows mixed results with baselines sometimes outperforming

Severe practical limitations: requires all modalities simultaneously (street view, satellite, OSM, POIs); computationally expensive (9× training overhead, Section H); limited investigation of incomplete modality scenarios
Narrow domain-specific contribution: highly specialized to urban geospatial analysis; generalizability to broader machine learning applications unclear; relevance to ICML community limited

Insufficient analysis: no investigation of failure cases, which geographic contexts work best/worst, when method fails, or actionable insights; synthetic data experiment (D.2.2) artificially perfect but real-world data likely more complex
Missing ethical considerations: no discussion of privacy implications, surveillance risks, or potential for algorithmic bias in urban prediction despite sensitive application domain

strengths: Novel Stochastic Multimodal Fusion framework that effectively captures redundant, unique, and synergistic information across modalities, with theoretical justification (Lemma 1) and empirical validation through synthetic data experiments

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation: 41 diverse urban prediction tasks across 56 cities worldwide with proper statistical controls, comprehensive ablation studies, and cross-regional generalization experiments
Robust to realistic incomplete modality scenarios (Table 6), maintaining strong performance even with 25% data availability, critical for real-world deployment
Excellent reproducibility: detailed implementation details, dataset construction protocols, hyperparameter specifications, code/model release planned, enabling future research
Clear practical contribution as first urban-specific multimodal location encoder addressing genuine gaps in geospatial ML for urban prediction tasks
Consistent performance improvements across diverse task domains (regression and classification) and geographic regions, demonstrating broad applicability
Strong theoretical grounding in information decomposition with partial information decomposition (PID) framework formalizing modality-specific, shared, and synergistic components
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: individual components (Vision Transformers, contrastive learning, reconstruction losses) are established techniques; random modality masking, while effective, is relatively straightforward
Task-specific improvements often modest (2-4% gains in R² over GAIR baselines on many tasks); missing analysis of when multimodal fusion is necessary vs. when single modalities suffice

Geographic bias in evaluation: heavy focus on developed nations (North America, Europe, wealthy Asia); limited evaluation in Global South, developing countries, or less-urbanized regions; generalization claims would benefit from more diverse evaluation

Incomplete theoretical justification: Assumption 1 (proxy modality existence) is strong and not universally validated; why random masking is optimal for information decomposition not thoroughly explained; temperature parameter τ appears empirically chosen without principled justification

Limited ablation studies on critical design choices: loss weight balance between contrastive and reconstruction objectives not systematically explored; masking probability not ablated; alternative Transformer fusion architectures not compared
Computational cost analysis limited to forward pass timing; training memory requirements unclear; scalability with very large modality vocabularies not addressed

No analysis of failure cases or task characteristics predicting when multimodal fusion helps most; some specialized baselines (e.g., PDFM for ZIP codes) outperform UrbanFusion on specific tasks without investigation

Statistical rigor gaps: linear probing results often lack confidence intervals despite MLP results including error bars; no formal statistical significance testing despite potential overlapping confidence intervals
Incomplete modality handling validated primarily through synthetic data; real-world missing data patterns (e.g., entire cities lacking street view) not thoroughly evaluated
